News.title: Labour urged to tackle crisis of jobless young people by cutting hiring costs
News.content:
LABOUR is being urged to tackle the crisis of jobless young people by cutting hiring costs.

Tax rises are making it hard for firms to employ them, according to MPs.





Higher minimum wages, National Insurance hikes and employment rights changes are hitting businesses.

The number of NEETs — young people not in education, employment or training — is close to a million.

Tory Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said: “Builders are desperate to hire [young people] but Labour have piled on costs that make it too expensive to give them a chance.

“You don’t fix youth unemployment by taxing the jobs they need. If we want our kids earning, we’ve got to cut the costs and stop pricing young people out of work.”

Reform’s Lee Anderson said: “All Labour has been successful at is destroying the job market while young people struggle to get a foot on the ladder.”

The Sun on Sunday’s Builder Better Britain campaign has helped secure youngsters placements in construction trades.

A Government spokesman said: “This Government inherited a dire shortage of construction workers and is determined to deliver more opportunities.

“That’s why our youth employment support package, totalling £2.5billion, includes the offer of £2,000 for each new employee aged 16 to 24 taken on by a small business, supporting almost one million young people and delivering up to 500,000 opportunities to earn and learn.”



They said those hiring under-21s earning below a certain level do not pay NI contributions.

News.title: Britain is at its weakest in 400 years – we need to prioritise bullets over benefits, Kemi Badenoch warns Starmer
News.content:
KEMI Badenoch has warned Britain is at its weakest in 400 years — as she pledged to go on the biggest ever peacetime rearming blitz.

The Tory leader said the UK has been “prioritising benefits over bullets” and is facing a day of reckoning.





Unleashing both ­barrels on PM Sir Keir Starmer, she branded his failure to find the billions needed to fund our military “a national disgrace”.

And she accused the Government of lying by ­pretending we are prepared for war, adding: “We are not ready.”

Ms Badenoch was speaking at the London Defence Conference, where she set out her plan to ramp up defence spending.

It came as the US and Iran held the first day of peace talks in Pakistan.



She said President Donald Trump had doled out some uncomfortable home truths — that Britain “cannot properly defend ourselves” without the US.

She said: “It is the culmination of long-standing policy failures which have left our defence capabilities arguably at their weakest in 400 years.

“I don’t need to tell you how this happened.

“Between 1989 and 2022, defence spending fell every year.



“We have grown fat on welfare. Prioritising benefits over bullets.”

The war in Iran exposed our shortcomings — with the UK unable to even send a warship to the region as missiles rained down on our allies and bases, she added.

Ms Badenoch said: “For a proud nation used to stamping its ­influence on the world, Britain’s lack of ­readiness for this war in Iran has been shocking.

“We weren’t just unprepared ­militarily, with no Royal Navy ­warships in the Middle East for the first time in decades. We were strategically unprepared too.”

Blame for this lies with the PM and not our brave Royal Navy, the Tory leader claimed.



She said Sir Keir has been too busy U-turning on benefits and caving to his rebellious backbenchers to prepare for war.

She said: “We have a Government that was politically unprepared for this war, distracted by its own infighting and psychodrama.

“The war in the Gulf must act as a wake-up call. Not for navel ­gazing or finger pointing about who did what, but for action.”

The Government-commissioned strategic defence review, co-authored by General Sir Richard Barrons, was published last year.

It set out the urgent rearming programme needed to make the UK war-ready.



But the Government has still not published the investment plan ­setting out how it will pay for higher defence spending.

Ms Badenoch branded this delay a “national scandal” and added: “Our Government literally doesn’t have a plan.”

Laying out her alternative defence spending blueprint, she promised to cut welfare and Net Zero projects to pay for weapons.

She said: “The next Conservative Government would reinstate the two-child benefit cap and spend that money on defence.

“That will fund the largest net increase in British troops under any Government since the Second World War. We will use the money to recruit 6,000 regular soldiers and 14,000 reservists — as well as paying for their accommodation and equipment.



“And we will reallocate £17billion from Government R&D [research and development work] and Ed Miliband’s disastrous Net Zero ­projects to create a new ­Sovereign Defence Fund.”

In a direct plea to the PM, she said the Tories will put party politics aside and unite with Labour to find cash for defence spending.

She said: “Let’s find the money to rearm. Let’s identify the ­spending cuts.

“And if we reach agreement on a joint plan, Conservatives will ­support those measures in ­Parliament on a three-line whip.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But No10 hit out at the ­Conservative leader’s offer.



A Downing Street spokeswoman said: “Kemi Badenoch sat around the Cabinet table when the Conservatives hollowed-out our Armed Forces. We have announced the biggest uplift in defence spending since the Cold War

“We won’t be taking any advice from her.”

News.title: Construction industry is crying out for young labourers… but Govt policies have priced youngsters out of jobs
News.content:
Shameful waste of Britain’s young

IT IS a national disgrace that a million youngsters are sitting on the scrapheap.

Nearly 13 per cent of all 16 to 24-year-olds are not in education or employment.



What makes this disaster even worse is that the construction industry is crying out for young labourers.



The Government’s ludicrously ambitious target of building 1.5million new homes by 2029 already looks like falling short by as much as a third.

Building firms need a quarter of a million new workers, like the youngsters we took to sites across the UK this week to get work experience.

So why can’t bosses plug their own gap and take 250k youngsters off the dole at the same time?

Because of the Government’s own ruinous policies of course.

They have priced youngsters out of jobs and tied employers in knots of red tape.

Under Labour’s increased minimum wage, firms simply can’t afford to train young people and the apprentice scheme is a sprawling mess.

This double failure is shameful.

It lets down a generation of youngsters who want to work but are confined to welfare, some for the rest of their lives.



And it is blocking the vital housing programme Britain so desperately needs.

Sir Keir Starmer is keen to trumpet the importance of Labour values.

What value is there in allowing this shambles to continue?

How many chances?

ANYONE who thinks our broken justice system is a recent phenomenon should study the insane case of rapist Neil Trennan.

This monster was first jailed for life in 1990 when he raped a woman after attacking her with a dumb-bell.



Yet in 2002 he was allowed day release, escaped from his supervisor and launched a sexually motivated attack on another woman, receiving a second life sentence.

In any normal system that would be enough to prevent him ever receiving leniency again.

But not in the opinion of the Parole Board, who recommended him for an open prison in 2023.

Astonishingly this fiend, who admitted he was addicted to sexual violence, was then allowed out on unsupervised day release, during which he absconded and tried to rape a third woman.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The judge who handed him a third life sentence in February is absolutely right to demand Justice Secretary David Lammy immediately investigate this outrage.



Mr Lammy must identify those responsible for letting this sex beast roam free and kick them out of the justice system.

News.title: Cruel words about late Queen are shameful and unnecessary – but evil specimen Andrew has made her an easy target
News.content:
IT is less than four years since the longest-reigning monarch in British history died.

But how quickly memories fade.



During that short time, some have forgotten all the good Queen Elizabeth II did during her 70 years on the throne.

They are also overlooking the respect she still deserves.

A new profile on her has been written in the (once!) respected Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, which is supposed to serve as a record of our notable public figures.



But it resembles something your average Gen Zer would put on TikTok.

It says the UK “ceased to be a great power in the world” under her.

It claims she adapted “slowly and not always enthusiastically” as Britain evolved into “a multicultural, multi-faith, multi-ethnic society”.

The biased anti-royalists wrote that she “had not been born to succeed” but by her “example, her self-discipline, her public spiritedness, and her longevity, she did so in more ways than one, living out perhaps the most remarkable life of her times.”

It makes her sound like a bigoted old aunt, forced into a job she didn’t want, but we just kind of tolerated her because she stuck around for so long.



This couldn’t be further from the truth. She was respected, loved and admired.

So many of the words seem cruel and unnecessary.

They have also chastised her “mis-steps” (particularly in relation to her family). And maybe here lies the real problem: Andrew.

Because of this vile specimen, who denies any wrongdoing, she has become an easy target. But just like us, the Queen didn’t know the truth before her death.

You don’t have to like the monarch to write about her.



But if you’re compiling her national biography profile, you should really make it your business to know what her role entailed.

A constitutional monarch serves as the ceremonial head of state.

Yes, the Prime Minister consults the monarch — and she would encourage and warn — but she didn’t make the political decisions that shape this country.

She graciously, invisibly, guided 15 Prime Ministers from the wings. (And how unsteady things have come without her presence.) This stabilising figure also urged, over many decades, people to embrace diversity, cultures, faiths and the Commonwealth.

As her job was to guide, not to tell us what to do, I am not quite sure how “enthusiastic” the authors of this barbed biography expected her to be.



Sense of duty

Her work was tireless, with 21,000 royal engagements in all.

She made friends along the way, from Nelson Mandela to comedian Billy Connolly, and showed her own great sense of humour in sketches with James Bond for the Olympic Games, with Paddington for her Jubilee.

She supported grandson Harry’s Invictus Games.

During Covid she remained strong and stabilising, telling us: “We will be with our friends again; we will be with our families again; we will meet again.”

She always led by example, always had a sense of duty.



Even at her husband’s funeral, when she sat alone to adhere to Covid distancing regulations.

We will never forget that haunting image of her with a black mask covering her pale face and just those glistening eyes visible above.

Our hearts went out to the nation’s grandmother and we wanted to console her.

Now is our chance to support her again.

Because so many of us do.



Half the country watched her funeral when she died.

And this month, as we celebrate what would have been her 100th birthday, let’s all pay our respects again.

Spread the positive truth about this great monarch to our own grandchildren so they hear about her from us, not that shameful biography.

We must cherish her great memory, not desecrate it.

I’M LOVING ANGEL’S EVERLASTING LOOK

THERE was a time when your granny looked, well, old. But how times have changed.



When Kate Jackson, Jaclyn Smith and Cheryl Ladd celebrated 50 years of TV show Charlie’s Angels this week, they could have passed for women decades younger. Especially Jaclyn.

She’s 80 and old enough to be my mother but could easily pass as my sister.

She maintains her ageless looks with a healthy lifestyle and diet, a good skin care routine and perhaps the key is that she uses her “own fat” for facial enhancement.



If that’s all it takes, lucky her. I’m all for a few tweakments when my credit card allows.

Now Jaclyn has become a pensioner influencer, other women might also want to hurtle towards an aesthetics clinic after collecting their bus pass.

But there’s only so much nipping and pricking you can do without looking ridiculous.

And Jaclyn has something most of us have never had – natural supermodel beauty, with flawless skin and cheekbones to die for.

She wouldn’t have got to say “Good morning” to Charlie for five years without those genes.



GROW UP, YOU BRATS

WHAT a disappointing pair of brats Sydney Sweeney and Zendaya have turned into.

They were once firm friends but Sydney is said to have flirted with Zendaya’s “is-he-isn’t-he-hubby” Tom Holland and they are also suffering from some sort of career rivalry.

But their career is acting – their current job is promoting their raunchy show Euphoria, and putting on a red-carpet performance is part of the job description.



Maybe they should have remembered that and acted like professional grown-ups, rather than refusing to even stand on it together at the premiere.

lTHERE is a strange new illness spreading around the pet world.

A study in the Netherlands has found that cat and dog owners are making false claims that their animals are sick – or even harming them – to seek attention from vets.

The majority of clinics there are familiar with the phenomenon.

The RSPCA says it’s also happening here despite huge vet bills.



These people have more money than sense.

READY, OR NOT

I’VE started a new health kick and it’s all thanks to Watford businessman Stephen Akuoko.

After reading about how he kept fish in a bath next his toilet before cooking them into ready-meals, I’ve gone right off convenience food.



All meals will now be cooked from scratch.

EGG ON THEIR FACES

IF you’ve been asked to look after something important by your boss that’s, say, priceless or even a collector’s piece, or for example a Faberge egg and watch set valued at up to £2.2million, what would you do with them to keep them safe?

A) Put them in an actual safe.



B) Keep them under your pillow.

C) Shove them in your bag and pop to the packed Dog and Duck pub in London’s Soho.

Oddly, Rosie Dawson opted for C.

Rosie was supposed to be guarding the Faberge items after taking them for display at a work event for her employers at the Craft Irish Whiskey Company.

But in the pub she put the bag down to greet a friend and quick-thinking thief Enzo Conticello swiped it – and its high-value goodies.



He flogged the lot to buy drugs and has been jailed for 27 months.

During his sentence he was told the theft had caused “inconvenience and stress” to Rosie and her company.

I imagine they all needed a stiff drink to get over that loss.

CHOC & CAW

STARS seemed to align last Sunday.

The weather in Manchester was good, I didn’t hit snooze on the 5.30am alarm, and hid chocolate all over my garden.



But 90 minutes later, when my seven-year-old went out with his basket, many of the foil-wrapped chocolate figures had disappeared.

It took a hunt of my own on our security camera to find the culprit . . . a great big thieving magpie.

Hope he was sick.

WHEN Greek prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis announced he was banning social media for teens to tackle anxiety and sleep problems, he added that “many of the younger ones among you will be angry with me”.

Now, yes, but they will thank him one day.

News.title: Sadiq Khan has to wake up… horror on Primrose Hill shows London I love is teetering on the edge of lawlessness
News.content:
IF Britain was not stark raving mad, we’d be honouring Walker Smith today.

Mr Smith, 54, tackled a shoplifter in Waitrose, his place of work for the last 17 years.





The man should have got a medal. Instead, he got the sack.

Because when Walker Smith saw some lowlife stuffing her bag with multiple Lindt Gold Bunny Easter eggs that she had not paid for, he intervened.

“I’ve seen it happen every hour of every day for the last five years,” he said.

“It’s everybody, from drug addicts to teenagers, nicking bits and bobs or walking out with bottles of wine in their arms. We’re not allowed to do anything.”

The cops, the courts and our political masters do not give a toss about shoplifting. But Walker Smith cared.

And caring cost this principled, decent man his job.

I have seen Mr Smith described as a security guard but that is incorrect. Walker was a shop assistant.

Security had been scaled back — “Because shoplifting incidents aren’t reported enough” — leaving non-security staff like Walker on the front line of the shoplifting plague.





So how can his employer imagine that he is the bad guy?

“There is a serious danger to life in tackling shoplifters,” simpered a witless Waitrose spokesperson.

“And that’s why we have policies in place that must be strictly followed.”

In other words — let the thieving bastards get away with it.

And Sir Sadiq Khan, Labour Mayor of London, has the brass neck to insist that the capital is “a safe city”.

Sadiq’s unconvincing evidence?

The cold comfort of knowing that London has a lower murder rate than “every state in the USA”.

As if having a lower homicide rate than gun-mad, psycho-stuffed America was a reason to break out the bubbly.

“Unfortunately, London-bashing has become something of a national and international sport with populist politicians, commentators and keyboard warriors trading in fear, not facts,” sighed Sadiq.

“We should be proud of how safe London is,” echoes Sir Mark Rowley, Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police.



But in the first few weeks of spring, horrific crimes have occurred all over the capital.

On Primrose Hill during a sunny afternoon, a 21-year-old man was stabbed to death.

Finbar Sullivan had taken his new camera — a 21st birthday present — to Primrose Hill to take some photographs. Finbar never came home.

Here was a gentle, creative young man who did his best to steer clear of trouble.

“When he got a scooter, he would ride to school and it would take him ages because he would avoid all the areas where there were gangs,” said Finbar’s heartbroken father, Chris Sullivan.

“He did not wear black because of that — he didn’t want to be associated with any gangs. He wore pale colours.”

Finbar knew all the dangers. It did not save him.

Just five days earlier, Eghosa Ogbebor was shot dead in Woolwich — another murder in broad daylight. Eghosa was 14.

In Golders Green, Jewish ambulances were firebombed.

And in Clapham, a mob of youths ran riot, ransacking shops and terrifying families.



And there is one reason for this social breakdown. There are far too many scumbags out there who believe that they are going to get away with their crime.

From shoplifting to carrying — and using — a deadly weapon.

From stealing Easter eggs to stealing phones to stealing some innocent boy’s life.

Running riot

Behind every single one of these crimes I guarantee that there is someone who thinks that they will never be punished.

Take your head out of the sand, Mr Mayor. Wake up and smell the sewer that our beloved London is becoming, Sir Mark.

This week the Met showed off its new fleet of armoured vehicles, £180,000 nine-tonne monsters called SandCats.

The money would have been better spent putting more old-school coppers on the street.

Because we desperately need a mayor who can see the heart-wrenching reality of crime running riot in the capital. We need cops who care, laws that bite, courts that are capable of making the scumbags fear that they will be punished.

The London I love is teetering on the edge of total lawlessness.



Sacked by Waitrose, Walker Smith has been offered a job by Lord Richard Walker, the boss of Iceland.

Lord Walker wants security guards to carry truncheons and pepper spray to fight shoplifting — that cosy euphemism for retail theft.

In Sainsbury’s, some security guards have been issued stab vests.

Costa Coffee has started having bouncers on the door across the capital to guard fridges.

Stab vests in Sainsbury’s! Bouncers in coffee shops!

There is not one worker in a London supermarket who does not feel that they are in mortal danger every day they go to work.

And Sadiq Khan complacently assures us London is a safe city?

Mr Mayor, you are out of your tiny mind.

Sydney to join the Q

HOLLYWOOD director Paul Feig suggests Sydney Sweeney should be the next James Bond.



“There have been some cool Bond girls,” says Paul, who directed El Syd in domestic thriller The Housemaid. “But come on! Let her be the super-spy. She’s great.”

Seems a bit of a long shot. But when Sweeney was once asked if she fancied being a Bond girl, she retorted: “I think I would have more fun as James Bond.”

She was not kidding. The Housemaid was shot for a reported $35million and has made about $399 million worldwide.

Which makes Sweeney the hottest star in Tinseltown. Could she really be the next 007?

With those kinds of figures at the box office, Sydney Sweeney can be whatever she likes.

WHEN they flew around the far side of the moon, the astronauts on Artemis II ventured deeper into space than anyone has ever been – 252,760 miles from Planet Earth.

An extraordinary moment for humanity.

And despite the calm, smiling competence of the crew, they were putting their lives at risk for every second.

The most memorable moment of my childhood was gazing up at the moon in the summer of 1969 and knowing that humans were walking on its surface. Isn’t it glorious to be back?

Trump fuels EU fans



THERE is a theory that Donald Trump is driving the UK back into the arms of the European Union. You can see the logic.

Most of us do not mind if the POTUS is rude about our socialist Prime Minister. We can’t stand him either.

But all of us feel our blood boil when the President is abusive about British Armed Forces.

In January Trump sneered that in Afghanistan – where the UK had 457 military deaths and thousands of our brave men and women suffered life- changing injuries – frightened Nato troops stayed “a little off the front line”.

Trump quickly retracted that lie. But his sneering has never really stopped. This President is too quick to casually call us cowards.

And disgustingly chummy with Russia’s Vladimir Putin.

A YouGov poll revealed that only 14 per cent of British people still believe we have a “special relationship” with America, 57 per cent want to get closer to the EU.

And if the European Union was smart, it would be wooing this country, and welcoming us back with open arms.

But it is not smart.

Watch the appetite for Rejoining shrivel when we contemplate the real cost. Finally giving up the pound for the euro.



Throwing open our borders and learning to love the Schengen Area.

Forgetting about the budget rebate negotiated by Margaret Thatcher.

And above all, bitterly regretting the error of our Brexit-voting ways and begging Europe for forgiveness.

This is what will stop us ever going back inside the EU. Brussels will want us to crawl.

Cheers Philip A NEW book, Queen Elizabeth II, by Hugo Vickers, describes in vivid detail the last night of Prince Philip’s life. Vickers reports that Philip “gave his nurses the slip, shuffled along the corridor on his Zimmer frame and helped himself to a beer”. The next morning the Duke quietly slipped away after a bath. He was 99 years old. That’s the way to go.

JOANNA LUMLEY, 79, joined a neighbour in confronting a gang of bikers attempting to steal her car from outside her home in Stockwell, South London.

The gang fled empty-handed when they saw the glint in Joanna’s eyes.

Which is possibly a bit of a surprise if you only know Lumley as pie-eye fashionista Patsy in Absolutely Fabulous.

But if you first saw her as karate-chopping, butt-kicking Purdey in The New Avengers, then it was totally in character.

I bet pet soon Fritz in with Heidi’s hubby

HEIDI KLUM steps out in New York with a mystery companion – a Yorkshire terrier mix called Fritz, who is from a pop-up adoption centre next to where the model and TV host was working.



“It took some convincing with my husband,” confesses Heidi.

Heidi’s husband will come around.

It is always the family member who is most resistant to the idea of getting a dog who falls most deeply in love with his new four-legged roommate.

News.title: How cut-price ‘direct cremations’ could lead to MORE monster funeral directors giving families wrong ashes
News.content:
FEARS are growing that cut-price “direct cremations” could encourage monsters like rogue funeral director Robert Bush.

One in five funerals now takes place without a service or mourners, with the ashes simply posted back to the grieving family.



After the horrific scandal of funeral director Bush, who this month pleaded guilty to giving families the wrong ashes and leaving bodies in his parlour for months, we can reveal there are fears rogue funeral directors could be disposing of bodies by putting two in a coffin to avoid paying cremation fees.

Rosie Inman-Cook, from charity The Natural Death Centre, says the unregulated industry is currently a “wild west of cowboys” who need no licence or qualifications to set up a funeral parlour.

‘Wild west of cowboys’

She said: “There’s nothing to stop any funeral director potentially putting two bodies in a coffin and cremating them together. The only way to prevent it is to legislate that when a coffin arrives at any cemetery, the lid has to be removed for the contents to be checked.



“This problem increases with direct cremation because there is no family there. And more and more people are choosing these.

“It’s a third of the cost of a regular cremation so families who are hard up are choosing that option.

“Some funeral directors tell ­relatives they are doing a cremation, but they don’t book it in and it doesn’t happen. They are given any old ash in a box, and told it is their loved one. Vulnerable people are being preyed upon.

“When a coffin arrives at a cemetery you trust the funeral director is being honest. They don’t take the lid off and look inside.

“If a family saw their tiny granny’s ­coffin and it’s 7ft foot long with six huffing and puffing pall bearers, they would suspect, but there’s a risk it could go unnoticed.



“Because there is no regulation, there’s nothing to stop gangsters and criminals setting up a funeral directors and disposing of people that way.”

Direct cremations can cost as little as £1,000 compared with £3,500 to £4,000 for a full ceremony, and are heavily advertised on TV and radio to the elderly as a low-cost way to avoid burdening loved ones with expensive funeral costs.

They represented 21 per cent of UK funerals last year, up from three per cent in 2019, according to a report from the insurer Sunlife.

As well as cost, the effect of the pandemic – when social distancing rules limited the number of people who could attend a service – has made them more common.

Adherence to a mandatory code of practice and licensing is law in Scotland under the Burial And Cremation Act 2016.



Funeral directors there are subject to mandatory, legally enforced regulations.

There are also strict requirements on washing, dressing and maintaining the dignity of the deceased, and inspections of facilities.

In England and Wales there are only voluntary schemes provided by trade bodies including the National Association of Funeral Directors, which has seen complaints more than double in the past three years from 231 in 2021/22 to 470 in 2024/25.



Bush, 47, gave relatives the wrong ashes while their loved ones’ bodies were left in his parlour for months.

Officers found 35 corpses and more than 100 sets of ashes at Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, in Hull, in March 2024.

One of the bodies had been there for a year.

After a guilty plea he will be sentenced in July.

Sets of ashes

In February, funeral directors ­Richard Elkin, and Hayley Bell were jailed for four years at Portsmouth Crown Court after leaving 46 bodies to decompose in a warm mortuary for more than a month, and ­were convicted of intentionally causing a public nuisance, preventing lawful burial, and carrying on business with intent to defraud creditors.



In January, undertaker Jack Weekes was convicted in Cornwall after keeping the body of an 86-year-old woman for more than a month after he should have cremated her.

He got 15 months, suspended for two years.

Michaela Baldwin’s stepdad was one of the victims involved in the Legacy Independent Funeral Directors case.

When she went there to say her last goodbye to stepdad Danny Middleton, she couldn’t help but notice the size of his coffin.

The former delivery driver, who was fond of ­Sunday roast dinners, had been a large man when he died in his 70s after long-term ill health relating to his heart.



Michaela, 35, a full-time mum, said: “When I saw the coffin I thought, ‘There is no way Danny can be in that’, but you are grieving. You think, ‘They’re the ­specialists, they know what they are doing’. He’s got to be in there. You only hear of that kind of stuff in horror films.”

The family had paid for a cremation, and were later given some ashes, which Danny’s nieces had been planning to turn into jewellery.



But in March 2024 Humberside Police revealed they were investigating the undertakers and the family got in touch.

They learned Danny’s body was still at the premises.

She says: “Danny ­was a wonderful man. He didn’t deserve this.

“When I eventually found out the truth, all I could think was, ‘Who the hell have we got? Who is this poor soul?’ We will never know.”



Funeral company Plan With Grace was recently fined because they posted ashes back to the wrong ­country.

A daughter, known as Mrs R, lodged the complaint with the financial ombudsman, after paying £1,440 for a direct cremation for her mother in 2024.

Her ashes were wrongly sent to an unnamed EU country.

By the time they arrived, there was “spillage and loss”.

The company tried to blame Royal Mail but the ombudsman ordered Plan With Grace to repay £1,000.



Rupert Callender, who runs the Green Funeral Company in Dartington, Devon, says hospitals are ­complaining about direct funerals, too.

He said: “A lot of the larger, more impersonal companies keep bodies in huge body hubs like some sort of grizzly Amazon warehouse.

“That disconnect means ­mistakes are bound to happen. Instead of undertakers, they have a guy with a van who drives around the hospitals collecting remains.

“Hospitals are exasperated because they’ve had to store bodies for weeks because direct companies have sold the family a funeral but not bothered to collect the body.”

Michaela is now campaigning for regulation and for “mandatory coffin inspections”.

News.title: Crypto-hunting gang hold terrified family at knifepoint and demand ‘key to millions’ in horror home invasion
News.content:
A WEALTHY businessman and his family were held at knifepoint in their home in a cryptocurrency robbery.

Oliver von Landsberg-Sadie, who founded leading London crypto firm the BCB Group, said the raiders demanded the keycode to his electronic wallet.





Stood next to an Aston Martin on his driveway, he told The Sun on Sunday: “They were only after crypto. They had no interest in my car.”

Oliver, 47, now chief of Greater Things, a multi-million-pound business using AI to launch tech firms, said four villains broke into his house in Maidenhead, Berks, and tied up him, wife Sarah and their two children.

South African Oliver said they were still shaken from their 10pm ordeal on April 2.

But he does not personally keep the digital money so the gang left disappointed.



However, they did nick cash, watches, and silver.

The day after, he warned other crypto tycoons online: “I was robbed at home at knifepoint last night, with my family, by four men looking for crypto specifically.

“There is clearly an organised campaign and I ask you to be more vigilant with your personal safety.”

He said: “It’s the sort of thing you see in the movies and never think will happen to you.



“They had no interest in the car, for example, because that’s traceable.

“Crypto is of course not the only thing burglars target but it’s true that it can be as vulnerable to theft as cash or jewellery if not kept securely.

“We live in a pretty safe country here but I’m from South Africa and nothing like this ever happened to me there.”

Thames Valley Police are hunting the culprits.

News.title: Person rushed to hospital after car smashes through window of Japanese restaurant
News.content:
DINER SCARE Person rushed to hospital after car smashes through window of Japanese restaurant

A PERSON is fighting for their life in hospital after a car ploughed into a Japanese restaurant in a town centre.

The Ford Kuga mounted the pavement and crashed into the window of the eatery in Wigston, Leicestershire.



Police, paramedics and fire crews all scrambled to Shokudo restaurant on Bell street just after 4pm today.



Leicestershire Police said one person in the building was rushed to hospital with “non-life threatening injuries”.

The driver and passenger of the car, a man and a woman both in their 80s, were unharmed in the crash.

One eye-witness told Leicestershire Live how they heard a loud bang while walking away from the restaurant.

“There’s extensive damage to the sushi shop.”

There have been no arrests in connection with the crash the force said.

A spokesperson added: “Officers are carrying out enquiries to ascertain the circumstances of the collision”.

They said: “Officers were called to the scene at 4.07pm this afternoon where a car – a Ford Kuga – has mounted the kerb and collided with a building.

“One person, who was inside the building, has been taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries. Two people – a man and a woman in their 80s – who were inside the car were not injured.



“No arrests have been made.

“Officers remain at the scene and in the immediate area carrying out enquiries to ascertain the circumstances of the collision, including CCTV checks.”

Officers have urged anyone with information to call the force on 101.

News.title: Imperial Leather stickers aren't just for decoration, they have useful function
News.content:
Imperial Leather stickers aren't just for decoration, they have useful function

For years, Imperial Leather soap has been a staple in British households, but many people are only just discovering the true purpose of the red and gold sticker

View 2 Images Despite, the cost of living shoppers continue to buy Imperial Leather thanks to its durability (Image: UIG via Getty Images)

Imperial Leather has been a trusted brand for generations. It was first introduced introduced by British company Cussons as a premium bar soap in 1878.

‌



However, the mass manufacturing in the 20th Century helped the soap to become a widely used household staple. Now part of PZ Cussons, Imperial Leather has broadened from bar soap into shower gels, hand washes and bath products, while continuing to trade on its long-running brand heritage.

‌



Drawing inspiration from the aroma of Russian leather - a formerly sought-after commodity - Imperial Leather soap was promoted for its longevity throughout the bleak period of World War II.

‌



With severe rationing in place, families needed to maximise their coupons, and therefore didn't want a soap that would merely dissolve after limited usage.

According to a wartime : "Imperial Leather Toilet Soap is one of the few luxuries still available to the discriminating. Supplies are obviously limited, but if only because Imperial Leather lasts longer and increases the purchasing power of your coupons, you should buy it wherever and whenever you can."

View 2 Images The robust metallic badge serves as a function in maintaining the bar's integrity (Image: Alamy Stock Photo)

‌



Imperial Leather packaging has long been built to signal traditional/premium. That’s why you typically see a crest/coat‑of‑arms motif, formal serif lettering, and wording that leans “classic” rather than trend-led.

The most recognisable packs use gold/amber as a base with deep red/burgundy accents, which look seriously classy.

Historically, the soap bars have been wrapped (often with a paper wrapper and/or carton) with the crest centred and the brand name large.

‌



The products are instantly recognisable thanks to their signature red and gold stickers. Yet, many might not know that this small emblem of excellence actually fulfils a functional role.

It turns out, the crest helps to keep the soap structurally in tact. One X user asked: "How does the sticker stay on Imperial Leather bars of soap right to the end?"

And in reply, a commenter said: "I believe you're supposed to have it in your soap dish/on the sink with the label side down. Stops soap getting a 'soggy bottom'."

Article continues below

This clarification was previously verified by an Imperial Leather spokesperson, who said the sticker prevents "mushiness" by working as a tiny built-in soap dish.

The official website adds: "Imperial Leather rests on its name. Did you know, our much-loved sticker also serves an important purpose? Please rest your soap on the sticker to help water drain away and help it last longer."

So there you have it, the sticker isn't just for decoration. It also helps to maintain the structural integrity of the bars of soap. You learn something new every day!

News.title: Schoolboy, 17, slaughters parents as astonishing plot to kill Trump uncovered
News.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Schoolboy, 17, slaughters parents as astonishing plot to kill Trump uncovered

In a case that shocked the US, a teen was found to have killed his parents to fund Trump assassination plot. Nikita Casap lived with their decomposing bodies for two weeks

View 5 Images A Wisconsin teen murdered his mother and stepfather — then stashed their bullet-riddled bodies under blankets and lived with the corpses for weeks, according to prosecutors. (Image: Waukesha County Jail)

It was unusual for Nikita Casap, 17, not to turn up at school. He had a perfect attendance record and good grades. Staff had called the home Casap shared with his mum, Tatiana, 35, and his stepfather Donald Mayer, 51, but there was no reply. Casap had come to the US with his mum from Moldova when he was a first grader. Tatiana had been married to Donald for nine years and they all lived in a large luxury home in Waukesha, Wisconsin.

‌



After two weeks of Casap not attending school, staff were so concerned that they called the police on February 28, 2025, and asked for a welfare check. Donald’s mum was also getting messages from her son that were not his usual tone or style. Donald’s boss had got a text on February 25 saying he was unwell but was also too unwell to talk.

‌



Sports star struggling with huge debt brutally guns down ex-wife's mum and dad READ MORE :

Officers went to the house and when they entered the property, there was a strong smell of decomposition. They discovered the dead bodies of Tatiana and Donald – they had been dead two weeks and had been shot. There was no sign of Casap, the family dog or Donald’s SUV.

‌



View 5 Images Nikita Casap, 17, appeared in court on a slew of charges, including first-degree intentional homicide, for the gruesome killings of his mom and stepdad in their Waukesha home (Image: Waukesha County Jail)

At first, it appeared that Casap could have been in danger, but the evidence at the scene pointed to him being the threat. He had shot his parents to death on, or around, February 11. Donald had been shot in the back of the head while working at his desk. Tatiana had been shot three times as soon as she’d walked through the door after returning home from a night class.

Camera footage proved that Casap had been living at the house with his parents’ bodies for two weeks. He filmed entering the room to light candles around the body of his stepdad who was covered in blankets and had been dead around a week at that point. Casap can be heard saying ‘So you can see him there. I can literally see the rotting body there.’ Surveillance footage from inside the home showed him entering the rooms where the bodies were – and he took photos.

‌



Casap had taken $14,000 in cash, passports, jewellery and the family dog, and had fled in Donald’s vehicle. Police circulated his details and he was apprehended in Kansas. Casap had the gun he’d used in clear view on the passenger footwell. While on the run, Casap had made several disturbing searches about serial killers and school mass shootings. But why had the perfect student killed his parents? The answer would be unbelievably shocking to everyone who worked on the case.

View 5 Images House of horrors. “The highest, highest counts that we have, quite frankly, in our country is what’s been alleged here,” Waukesha County Commissioner David Herring said in court, WISN reported. (Image: WISN)

Police discovered that Casap had killed his parents as part of an elaborate plot to assassinate President Donald Trump. In late 2024. Casap had written a manifesto outlining the need for Trump’s death and how he wanted to overthrow the US government. At first the mission was to target Trump with an AK-47 rifle attached to a drone, then he decided he wanted to drop explosives from a drone – he said he didn’t care how many people got hurt in the attack.

‌



Casap had been communicating with two people online who said they felt the same way. Police found messages on his phone showing he was in touch with someone who spoke Russian. Casap had sent them $8,700 in Bitcoin from his stepdad’s account to pay towards a drone and explosives which was needed for the plot – but it was going to cost more.

It was determined that Casap had killed his parents to get more money. Casap spoke to the Russian contact, asking how long he would have to hide before he would flee by ship to Ukraine. When interviewed by police, Casap said he had been waiting for instructions on how the assassination was going to be carried out when he did ‘the Tuesday thing.’ That was a reference to killing his parents.

Investigators looked into the alleged plot to kill Trump and discovered that Casap had been scammed. The whole plan was a hoax to get money from Casap – they saw him as an easy mark and never intended on providing a drone or explosives. After further investigation, no further arrests were made. At no point had they instructed Casap to kill his parents.

‌



View 5 Images The court heard how Casap had decided to kill his parents for financial reasons (Image: AP)

In January this year, Casap pleaded guilty to two counts of first-degree murder. Prosecutors dropped seven other charges as part of a plea deal, including two counts of hiding a corpse and theft. In March this year, Casap, 18, was sentenced. The convictions automatically carried a life sentence, but the judge would decide whether there was a chance of parole.

The court heard how Casap had decided to kill his parents for financial reasons and not at the request of two scam artists. ‘Never at any time did any of these people say 'you need to kill your parents.' It appears that was the defendant's plan,’ the prosecution said. ‘I don't know how that works into attacking a politician, but for him, he believed he needed to kill his parents before he left the residence.’

‌



Casap’s lawyer said that the teenager had heard news of a doctor who drove his car into a Christmas market in Magdeburg, Germany, in December 2024 and had killed six people. It had angered him so much, he decided to act and had started to visit chatrooms. The two people he had contacted convinced him that he was part of a larger military strategy. Casap made a statement. ‘What I did was vile,’ he said. ‘What I did was thoughtless. What I did was wrong… I thought I was part of a revolution. Part of a war. And I told myself that bad things had to happen in war.’

View 5 Images The judge called the crime ‘horrific’ and ‘inexplicable.’ He handed Casap two life sentences with no chance of parole. (Image: WDJT)

Donald’s brother Robert Kitchell said he spoke on behalf of the entire family who was all grieving over the double loss. ‘Their lives were taken in an act of senseless and unforgiveable violence,’ Robert said. ‘For more than a year, we have struggled to make sense of it. There is no reason that can justify such an ultimate dread. My family is forever broken. There will never be another holiday, celebration or gathering where we are whole again.’

Article continues below

The judge called the crime ‘horrific’ and ‘inexplicable.’ He handed Casap two life sentences with no chance of parole. It’s unclear why Casap didn’t just take money from his parents – they didn’t need to die. Perhaps they had found out about the money he’d already stolen or they’d discovered his plans. Whatever the case, two innocent people lost their lives in a completely senseless attack. Casap did end up making headlines but not in the way he expected.

News.title: Haiti citadel: At least 30 dead in stampede at popular tourist attraction in Haiti
News.content:
Haiti citadel: At least 30 dead in stampede at popular tourist attraction in Haiti

A popular tourist attraction in the Caribbean state, and was packed with students and visitors ⁠on Saturday when a horror stampede killed at least 30 people

View 2 Images The stampede occurred at ⁠the Laferriere Citadel, a 19th-century fortress (Image: x.com/josephlunieOFF)

At least 30 people have been killed after a stampede in Haiti, but authorities ‌are warning the death toll could rise.

‌



Authorities said the stampede occurred at ⁠the Laferriere Citadel, a 19th-century fortress is one of the most popular tourist attractions in the Caribbean state, and was packed with students and visitors ⁠on Saturday when the horror stampede happened.

‌



Haitian Prime Minister, Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, confirmed that "many young people" were in attendance, but did not identify the victims or give an estimate of the death toll. In a statement, he extended "his sincere condolences to the bereaved families and assures them of his profound solidarity during this time of mourning and great suffering".

‌



View 2 Images Haitian Prime Minister, Alix Didier Fils-Aimé (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Jean Henri Petit, head of civil protection for Haiti's Nord Department, said the disaster occurred at the entrance to the site and was further exacerbated by rain.

Article continues below

The Caribbean country has been afflicted by violent gangs in recent years with including up to 90% of the capital, Port-au-Prince, according to UN figures.

Armed with trafficked weapons, they terrorise civilians with murder, kidnapping, and sexual violence. Recent disasters have also taken their toll, including fuel tank explosions in 2021 and 2024, that killed 90 and 24 people respectively, and a 2021 earthquake that left some 2,000 people dead.

News.title: Ryanair reminds passengers of new digital rule ahead of summer holidays
News.content:
Ryanair reminds passengers of new digital rule ahead of summer holidays

Ryanair is reminding passengers about its digital-only policy that came into effect in November 2025

View 3 Images Ryanair confirmed the changes when it came into force in November 2025 (Image: Getty)

Ryanair is alerting travellers to a change to its boarding passes, encouraging them to prepare in advance.

‌



The airline's Help Centre confirmed it has transitioned to entirely digital boarding passes, a shift that came into effect on November 12, 2025. A notice on Ryanair's homepage displays a banner, reminding passengers of the new system.

‌



On another page, it confirmed: "Ryanair has moved to 100% Digital Boarding Pass. This means all passengers will recieve a DBP to their Ryanair App when they check-in online.

‌



"Online check-in can be completed on Ryanair.com or on the Ryanair App. You need the Ryanair App to access your digital boarding pass."

How does it work?

View 3 Images Ryanair have a banner displayed on its website reminding customers of the change (Image: Ryanair)

Check-in online on Ryanair.com or Ryanair App prior to arriving at airport.

After check-in your DBP will appear automatically in your Ryanair App.

Present your DBP at airport security & at the boarding gate for your flight.

Once you have checked-in online, your DBP will be available offline in the Ryanair App.

‌



Why have Ryanair gone 100% digital for its boarding passes?

Lowers airport costs and fares for all Ryanair passengers

Provides a better service (including flight info) for customers on the day of travel

Improves customer service and re-booking during flight disruptions

Better for our environment - the airline said it "gets rid of 300 tonnes of paper annually."

Ryanair have confirmed check-in and ticket desks will remain available at all airports.

Discussing check-in, Ryanair say that all "passengers will still receive email reminders to check-in online 48 and 24 hrs pre-departure. If any passenger arrives at the airport but hasn’t checked-in online (having ignored these reminders), they will still be required to pay the airport check-in fee."

What happens if I lose my smartphone or tablet or it dies?

Ryanair has confirmed that if you've "already checked-in online and your smartphone or tablet is lost, you will receive a free of charge boarding pass at the airport."

‌



The same thing will happen if your smartphone or tablet dies, and you have already checked-in online.

I don't have a smartphone or tablet

Ryanair says: "If passengers don’t have a smartphone or tablet, as long as they have already checked-in online before arriving at the airport, they will receive a free of charge boarding pass at the airport.

"However, they will not be able to access real-time flight updates or benefit from enhanced customer service during any flight disruptions."

‌



Do I need to pay a boarding pass re-issue fee?

"Thanks to DBP, boarding pass re-issue fees will disappear as long as you have checked-in online prior to arriving at the airport", the airline confirmed.

What happens if I don’t check-in online before arriving at the airport?

View 3 Images Ryanair has reminded passengers of the update (Image: IDRISS BIGOU-GILLES/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images)

"You will be required to pay the airport check-in fee", Ryanair said.

Article continues below

Concluding its advice, the airline urges people to "please download the Ryanair App, if you haven’t already. It’s the only way to access your digital boarding pass."

News.title: Ryanair and easyJet flight warning as exact date airports face fuel shortages revealed
News.content:
Ryanair and easyJet flight warning as exact date airports face fuel shortages revealed

Major UK airlines have warned that should the Strait of Hormuz not be fully reopened in the coming weeks then fuel shortages will have an impact of travel ahead of the summer holidays

View 2 Images Airlines give warnings as fuel shortages faced by EU airports

European airports will face "systemic” shortages of fuel if the Strait of Hormuz is not fully reopened within three weeks, experts have warned.

‌



ACI Europe, which represents EU airports, noted that jet fuel reserves were running low with further supplies strained due to “the impact of military activity on demand”.

‌



Despite a current ceasefire and negotiations of a deal underway, there will still be 'ripple effects' for airlines as the impact of reduced gas supplies was felt worldwide.

‌



With JD Vance announcing today "no deal" has been reached yet, it means that the impact could be felt as early as the week of May 4.

View 2 Images European airports will face "systemic” shortages of fuel if the Strait of Hormuz is not fully reopened (Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)

A letter seen by the Financial Times, warned “increasing concerns of the airport industry over the availability of jet fuel as well as the need for proactive EU monitoring and action”.

‌



“If the passage through the Strait of Hormuz does not resume in any significant and stable way within the next three weeks, systemic jet fuel shortage is set to become a reality for the EU,” the letter said.

Although major airlines still have weeks of supply left, the upcoming peak summer season raises further concerns about supply and costs.

Ryanair has warned that if the war doesn't end this month, there will be disruption from May.

‌



Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary said: "Fuel suppliers are constantly looking at the market. We don't expect any disruption until early May, but if the war continues, we do run the risk of supply disruptions in Europe in May and June, and we hope the war will finish sooner than that and the risk to supply will be eliminated.

"We think there is a reasonable risk, some low level, maybe 10 per cent to 25 per cent of our supplies might be at risk through May and June, so like everyone else in this industry, we hope the war ends sooner rather than later.

"If the war finishes by April and the Strait of Hormuz reopens, then there is almost no risk to supply."

‌



Despite the confidence that should negotiations be made, travel will not be under threat, it is reported that suppliers are unable to guarantee deliveries into May.

This week European jet fuel prices hit a record $1,900 per metric ton, according to specialised publication Argus.

The hike could see potential shortfalls coming in future months.

Article continues below

Kenton Jarvis, the boss of EasyJet, warned that pricing was “volatile” since this “terrible war started” however the company is "well hedged" in terms of supplies.

The likelihood of cancellations comes after four Italian airports last weekend introduced restrictions on jet fuel after disruption. Air New Zealand also cancelled a selection of flights due to high fuel prices.

News.title: Four common foods Dr Michael Mosley warned us about
News.content:
Four common foods Dr Michael Mosley warned us about

The late Dr Michael Mosley shared advice on so-called healthy foods

View 2 Images Dr Michael Mosley (Image: Brook Mitchell, Getty Images)

The late Dr Michael Mosley warned his followers about a number of so-called "healthy" foods that may not be as beneficial as we might believe. Before his tragic death in 2024, the fitness and nutrition expert shared a wealth of health guidance across his social media channels, through his Just One Thing podcast and his numerous books.

‌



With supermarket shelves laden with products claiming to be the best choices for those watching their weight, it can be difficult to distinguish which ones live up to their promises. According to the health expert, many of these foods fail to deliver the nutritional benefits they advertise and may do "more harm than good".

‌



Writing on the Fast 800 blog in 2023, Dr Mosley said: "In a world full of food manufacturers, with clever marketing and a lack of science behind their claims, it can often become confusing to know exactly which foods are healthy when you're navigating the supermarket.

‌



"With huge signs at the end of each aisle, telling you exactly why the latest products will turn your health around, it's easy to fall into their well set traps and spend a fortune on "healthy" foods that are not so healthy."

The popular doctor outlined four foods that are marketed as healthy, but which he advised consumers to think twice about purchasing, as reported by the Daily Record.

Four 'healthy' foods to look out for

Low-fat products

‌



Low-fat snacks have long been the first port of call for anyone on a health kick. However, in recent years, scientific studies have produced a wealth of fresh evidence highlighting the health advantages of full-fat products. Michael has outlined several reasons why low-fat options may not be the healthiest choice.

He explained that low-fat products are frequently depleted of their nutrients and packed with sugar and additives to compensate for the taste lost by removing the fat. These sugar-heavy, low-fat items can trigger blood sugar spikes, intensifying cravings and leading to energy crashes.

View 2 Images You may think you're choosing a healthier option if you go for low-fat (Image: Getty)

‌



Furthermore, Michael pointed out that consuming foods abundant in mono and poly-unsaturated fats deliver rich flavour while maintaining satiety and they may even support weight reduction. He said: "A study, carried out by researchers at Stockholm's Karolinska Institute, tracked the diets of 20,000 women over a period of 20 years.

"The study found links between the consumption of full-fat dairy products (milk and cheese) and weight loss. Over a ten year period, the women who regularly consumed full-fat milk saw a lower [Body Mass Index] BMI."

Vegetable crisps

‌



In recent years, veggie crisps have emerged as a fashionable alternative to traditional potato versions. But according to Dr Mosley, these slim vegetable slices aren't substantial enough to deliver any genuine nutritional benefit.

With most being fried in sunflower oil to achieve their crispiness and coated in salt for additional taste, he suggested they may be no more wholesome than those crafted from potatoes. If you're after something crunchy and savoury to keep you going until dinner, the health expert suggests choosing raw vegetables, nuts, seeds, or gut-boosting sauerkraut and kimchi.

Bottled salad dressings

‌



Salads ought to be helping you reach your health goals, but Michael said they could be why you're struggling to see results, thanks to their dressings. He said: "Not only do commercial dressings have a significant amount of calories per serving (and not many of us actually stick to the recommended serving of one tablespoon), they're also packed with additives, to extend their shelf life, thickeners, hidden and other nasties that simply don't belong in your cupboard!"

Rather than processed dressings, have a go at making your own with equal parts olive oil to balsamic vinegar or lemon juice.

Flavoured porridge

Article continues below

A bowl of homemade porridge prepared with rolled oats and whole milk is a brilliant way to kick off the day, but the same can't be said for those "just add water" sachets.

According to Michael, one bowl of instant oatmeal can contain up to three spoonfuls of sugar, as some brands have a whopping 16g per serving.

News.title: Beloved theme park open for 41 years 'now looks like Chernobyl' after being abandoned
News.content:
Beloved theme park open for 41 years 'now looks like Chernobyl' after being abandoned

A theme park loved by British families that opened 50 years ago in 1976 is now a shell of its old self after it was forced to shut following several incidents of anti-social behaviour

View 8 Images The Children’s Pleasure Park now looks totally different (Image: The Bearded Explorer/YouTube)

A theme park that first opened exactly 50 years ago is now completely abandoned — despite once being a favourite for British families.

‌



The Children’s Pleasure Park in Southampton was the brainchild of grandparents Donald and Betty Slater, who launched it way back in 1976.

‌



However, they both died in 2014, and the park, which was given to their two sons, later suffered arson attacks and became a hub for anti-social behaviour.

‌



It now stands eerily empty having closed in 2017. While many of the beloved 20 attractions remain in place, a lot of the infrastructure is rotting, and much of the space on Golf Course Road in Bassett, Southampton, is completely overgrown with plants.

One urban explorer, Colin Smith, who is known online as The Bearded Explorer, took a trip to the once bustling theme park late last year, before documenting what he found.

View 8 Images The Bearded Explorer has 262,000 subscribers on YouTube (Image: The Bearded Explorer/YouTube)

‌



Sharing his thoughts, he said: “It’s quite sad actually. I should imagine there’s many happy memories that have been made in here when this place was active. But sadly, now it’s completely abandoned.”

He soon added: “This is almost a bit like Chernobyl, you know the fairground that was in Chernobyl? Just how derelict it was. I mean, this is exactly the kind of feeling I’m getting in this place.”

Despite this, he said the theme park was still incredible to see, and said some of the rides were exactly the same as he remembered from when he was a youngster.

‌



View 8 Images How it looks now (Image: The Bearded Explorer/YouTube)

The theme park had a reputation for being more affordable than the bigger named ones. There was no entry fee, and kids were free to turn up to have fun. Families were also encouraged to bring picnics where they could eat on tables and benches.

Colin took a visit with his daughter and he highlighted all that remained including the huge bumpy slide, swing boats, a helter-skelter, a colourful merry-go-round, a mini-train, a Formula One track and a tuck shed.

‌



He noted that it was quite a small space and that it must have felt quite claustrophobic for visitors.

View 8 Images How it once looked (Image: The Bearded Explorer/YouTube)

And taking it all in, he said: “This brings back so many memories. All this sort of stuff, you know, when I was a kid, it was all obviously quite new and well used. You pretty much saw this everywhere.

‌



“Any theme park you went to, any funfair at the seaside or anything like that, this was the kind of stuff that you would have seen.”

He also popped into the token shed where things like ice creams used to be sold and there were still newspaper clippings stuck up on the walls, as a reminder to the history of the theme park.

View 8 Images Colin said it left him feeling sad but also nostaligic (Image: The Bearded Explorer/YouTube)

‌



And again speaking about the downfall, Chris said: “Oh, it is a real shame this. Like I said before, there must have been so many happy memories made in here.

“And this place now, it’s just going to be demolished. It is one of those things, you know, life moves one. People build places all over the place and little businesses like this sadly just can’t sustain now.”

He later added: “It does make me sad that places like this have to one day disappear and that’s exactly what’s going to happen to this place — it is only a matter of time now.”

‌



View 8 Images The old boat swings (Image: The Bearded Explorer/YouTube)

Founder Donald was a grandad-of-six when he and his wife Betty opened the Children’s Pleasure Park half-a-century ago.

He was an experienced trampoline instructor and hand-built many of the rides himself.

‌



Donald and Betty ran it for almost four decades before they handed the reins over to their sons.

However, in 2014, Betty passed away, before Donald died just days later, and despite their good run, the theme park they built from scratch now lies in ruins.

View 8 Images Donald and Betty pictured together at the park (Image: The Bearded Explorer/YouTube)

‌



An arson attack took place in December 2021, one of several incidents of vandalism and destruction. Donald’s sons, Gary and Andrew, told the Daily Echo at the time: “This park is my life’s work and I’ll be very upset if it has to close down.”

A GoFundMe was launched to try and save it, and Andrew, who worked there for nearly 47 years, added: “It is such a special and wonderful place for the Southampton community. Anyone you speak to in Southampton, they’ve all been there.”

Sadly, the park closed for good in recent times, and one comment on The Bearded Explorer’s video, which you can watch in full here, revealed what may happen to it in the future.

Article continues below

View 8 Images It will be transformed in the future (Image: The Bearded Explorer/YouTube)

It read: “The Southampton City Council are now, at long last, spending millions getting the whole site modernised. No houses but new sports pavilions.”

However, a spokesperson for Southampton City Council told us: “Work is underway to consider future plans for the site, and updates will be shared if and when further information is available. At present, there are no details to confirm or comment on.”

News.title: Trump booed during 'pathetic' UFC entrance as Iran peace talks stall
News.content:
Trump booed during 'pathetic' UFC entrance as Iran peace talks stall

US President Donald Trump was booed as he made his entrance at UFC 327 in Miami on Saturday, with the president's approval ratings still at a record low in the wake of the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran

View 2 Images (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

President Donald Trump was met with boos as he made his entrance at UFC 327 in Miami, as his vice president, JD Vance, announced peace talks with Iran had stalled.

‌



It marked the first sporting event the president had attended since the US-Israel conflict with Iran erupted at the end of February - and comes at a time when his approval ratings have plummeted to record lows.

‌



Social media users were quick to react to the reception he received.

‌



"Trump walking in with Dana White to this empty UFC event is about as pathetic as it gets," wrote one social media user.

"Holy s***, Trump getting booed like that at a UFC event is a MASSIVE change to the publics perception of him," another added.

A third suggested the president being booed was a sign that "the world is healing.

‌



"Donald Trump got booed during his UFC entrance at this Buffalo Wild Wings, the world is healing," they wrote.

View 2 Images (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Ahead of the event, UFC chief executive Dana White confirmed Trump's attendance during a live stream alongside internet personality Adin Ross.

‌



"We've got the big guy coming on Saturday, too," White said. "Yeah, he's coming."

The president had also been present the last time UFC visited Miami in April 2025, when he was welcomed with a standing ovation and chants of "USA!" Trump attended a UFC 302 event in June 2024 shortly after being found guilty of 34 felony counts of fraud by a New York jury. While the convictions had left Trump in a precarious political position, the reception he received at the event in Newark, N.J., demonstrated that he retained considerable backing amongst ordinary Americans.

Trump went on to win the 2024 presidential elections and re-entered the White House in January 2025.

Article continues below

It comes as JD Vance announced no agreement has been made with Iran after 21 hours of negotiations, citing their nuclear ambitions as a key blocker for peace.

Talks between the US and Iran took place in Pakistan’s capital, Islamabad, over the weekend, with the vice president leading the US delegation.

"The bad news is we have not reached an agreement," Vance told reporters.

News.title: Iran chose 'not to accept our terms', Vance says after negotiations
News.content:
Vice-President JD Vance has said that the US and Iran failed to reach an agreement following lengthy peace talks in Pakistan.

The delegations met in Islamabad, Pakistan during a temporary ceasefire.

Vance said the US "could not get to a situation where the Iranians were willing to accept our terms". Halting Iran's nuclear capabilities had been a "core goal" that wasn't reached.

Iran's foreign ministry says the talks were "intensive", and called on Washington to refrain from "excessive demands and unlawful requests".

News.title: 'It's a special thing to be on Planet Earth': Artemis crew welcomed home in Houston
News.content:
The four astronauts who flew in Nasa's Artemis II mission around the Moon have been welcomed back to Planet Earth at an event in Houston, Texas.

Commander Reid Wiseman said the mission was "the most special thing I ever went through in my life".

The astronauts - Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, mission specialist Christina Koch and Canadian astronaut Jeremy Hansen - were all reunited with their families on Saturday.

Their nine-day voyage took them further from Earth than any humans in history.

News.title: Grand National 2026: I Am Maximus becomes two-time winner
News.content:
I Am Maximus became the first horse since Red Rum in 1977 to regain the Grand National as trainer Willie Mullins celebrated his third consecutive victory in the race at Aintree.

The 2024 winner and last year's runner-up came into the race as the 9-2 favourite and backed that up by finishing ahead of Iroko, Jordans and Johnnywho.

It made Irishman Mullins, who won the race for a fourth time in total, the first trainer since Vincent O'Brien between 1953 and 1955 to win in three successive years.

The feat means that JP McManus is now the leading owner in the history of the race with four wins - backing up the victories of Don't Push It in 2010, Minella Times in 2021 and I Am Maximus in 2024.

McManus could also boast owning three of the top four in Saturday's showpiece race, with only Jordans not in his stable.

Red Rum's second and third victories came in 1974 and 1977, and I Am Maximus is the first horse to have won the race in non-consecutive years since.

Further history for I Am Maximus was made by him, with a handicap of 11st 12lbs, becoming the first top weight to win since Red Rum carried 12 stone to victory in 1974.

Jockey Paul Townend said he felt "privileged" to be riding I Am Maximus.

He told ITV: "He's tough. He's a really, really good horse, and although Grangeclare West and Nick Rockett looked good in training, this lad wasn't telling me not to ride him.

"He is so good and has such an engine. He will gallop to the end of the world for you. I am really privileged. What a horse.

"Grand Nationals and Gold Cups are the pinnacle of the sport and I have them both."

Cate Blanchett, Bryan Cranston and Paddington Bear are among the contenders on Sunday at London’s Olivier Awards, which celebrate achievements in theater, opera and dance.

“Ted Lasso” star Nick Mohammed hosts the 50th anniversary edition of the awards at a star-studded ceremony at the Royal Albert Hall, where Ian McKellen, Helen Mirren, Vanessa Williams and Andrew Lloyd Webber will be among the trophy presenters.

Leading the nominations for Britain’s equivalent of Broadway’s Tony Awards, with 11 apiece, are homegrown heart-warmer “Paddington: The Musical” and a much-praised revival of Stephen Sondheim’s twisted fairy tale journey “Into the Woods."

Acting nominees include Marianne-Jean Baptiste, Paapa Essiedu, Rosamund Pike, Tom Hiddleston, Blanchett — for playing a vain actor in Anton Chekhov’s “The Seagull” — and Cranston for his performance as a troubled patriarch in Arthur Miller’s “All My Sons.”

The category of best actor in a musical includes a joint nomination for James Hameed and Arti Shah, who together play the titular marmalade-loving Peruvian bear in “Paddington.” Hameed provides the voice and remote puppetry, while Shah inhabits the bear costume onstage.

The ceremony will include performances from nominated musicals and numbers marking two significant anniversaries: 40 years of Lloyd Webber’s “Phantom of the Opera,” and 20 years of “Wicked” in the West End.

Stage star Elaine Paige, who is known for her leading roles in hit musicals including “Cats,” “Evita,” “Sunset Boulevard” and “Piaf,” will receive this year’s Special Award.

The Olivier Awards were founded in 1976 and named after the late actor-director Laurence Olivier. The winners are chosen by voting groups of stage professionals and theatergoers.

London’s West End is celebrating a strong post-pandemic return, buoyed by new musicals such as “Paddington” and “The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry,” and revivals including director Jamie Lloyd’s bold staging of “Evita.”

The Society of London Theatre, an industry umbrella group, says ticket sales have surpassed the levels seen before the COVID-19 pandemic. Shows in the West End — the collective name for London's theaterland — attracted 17.6 million visitors in 2025, 3 million more than Broadway.

But there are concerns about rising ticket prices and soaring production budgets, fueled by higher costs for labor, materials and energy.

“Theaters are busier than ever, but many are operating with far less financial headroom,” the society said in a report published last month.

The Artemis II astronauts received a hero’s welcome on Saturday as they returned to their Houston base after splashing back down to Earth a day earlier.

The crew of four arrived at Ellington Field near NASA's Johnson Space Center and Mission Control, flying in from San Diego, where they landed in the Pacific the evening before.

After a quick reunion with their spouses and children, the astronauts took the hangar stage, surrounded by space center workers and other guests.

The crowd included NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, flight directors and the launch director, Orion capsule and exploration system managers, high-ranking military officers, the space agency’s entire blue-suited astronaut corps and even retired ones, and more.

“Welcome home Artemis II,” Isaacman announced.

open image in gallery ( AFP/Getty )

Commander Reid Wiseman and his U.S.-Canadian crew's homecoming was poignant: They returned to their Houston home base on the 56th anniversary of the launch of Apollo 13, whose “Houston, we’ve had a problem” refrain turned a near-disaster into triumph.

During Artemis II's nearly 10-day mission, they voyaged deeper into space than the moon explorers of decades past and captured views of the lunar far side never witnessed before by human eyes. A total solar eclipse added to the cosmic wonder.

On their record-breaking flyby, the astronauts reached a maximum 252,756 miles (406,771 kilometers) from Earth before hanging a U-turn behind the moon, eclipsing Apollo's 13 distance record.

The mission also revealed a new side of our planet with an Earthset photo, showing our Blue Marble setting behind the gray, pockmarked moon. The image echoed the famous Earthrise shot from 1968 taken by the world’s first lunar visitors, Apollo 8.

open image in gallery NASA Artemis Moonshot ( NASA )

Despite the accomplishments, Artemis II astronauts had to contend with a more mundane problem — a malfunctioning space toilet. NASA promised a design fix before longer moon-landing missions.

Wiseman, pilot Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Canada's Jeremy Hansen were the first humans to fly to the moon since Apollo 17 closed out NASA's first exploration era in 1972. Twenty-four astronauts flew to the moon during Apollo, including 12 moonwalkers.

Apollo 13 commander Jim Lovell — who also flew on Apollo 8 — cheered the Artemis II crew on in a wake-up message recorded before he died last summer.

It was crucial for NASA that Artemis II go well. The space agency is already preparing for next year's Artemis III, which will see a new crew practice docking its capsule with a lunar lander in orbit around Earth. That will set the stage for the all-important Artemis IV moon landing in 2028, when two astronauts attempt a touchdown near the lunar south pole.

The Associated Press contributed to this report

News.content:
